--------
Rex Holloway speaks with Vlad about prison politics inside the Aryan Brotherhood, explaining how members and associates were expected to prove their status on Texas units. Recalling his time as a senior lieutenant at the Torres Unit in Hondo, Texas, Holloway says inmates claiming affiliation had to produce references through the chain of command, answer inside questions, and follow strict procedures to avoid being targeted. He describes how guards, gang intelligence, strip searches, solitary confinement, and the lack of visible patches shaped Aryan Brotherhood communication and identification behind bars. Holloway also discusses “hang around” associates, commissary weapons, steel-toe boots, and the consequences for members who failed to share prison contraband profits, including tobacco and drugs allegedly brought in by corrupt officers. The conversation offers a firsthand look at prison gang hierarchy, loyalty, verification, and survival in the Texas correctional system.

Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza speaks with Vlad about the early Mexican Mafia street killings he says he was tied to, including a retaliation mission in Bakersfield, Kern County, connected to the death of Cheyenne Gardena, portrayed in *American Me*. Mendoza describes targeting Nuestra Familia member Danny “Woodsy” Reyes after prison remarks about Cheyenne, using Gloria Perez, aka Cyclone, to gain access to the home. He recounts the chilling hours spent inside after Ronnie Reyes was killed, waiting for Woodsy to return while fearing innocent witnesses could walk in. Mendoza also discusses internal Mexican Mafia rules about avoiding law enforcement and civilians, Cyclone’s alleged role in the execution, and two other early killings involving his brother Angel, Joe Morgan, BGF, Helen Moresby, Bob Moresby, Artie from King Cobras, and Huntington Park. A rare firsthand account of prison politics, street enforcement, and organized crime history.

--------
Denvonta “Dirt Rocc” Lee sits down with VladTV to discuss the surprising outcome of Keefe D’s murder trial in the killing of 2Pac Shakur. After testifying in the case, Dirt Rocc says he believed Keefe D still had a reasonable chance at an acquittal or at least a hung jury, especially under Nevada’s unanimous verdict rules. Vlad compares that view with Judge Mathis, who also questioned whether prosecutors had overcome reasonable doubt, citing issues like no weapon and difficulty placing Keefe D at the scene. Dirt Rocc recalls learning the guilty verdict came back in just 90 minutes and explains why such a fast decision suggested jurors had already made up their minds. The conversation also covers jury makeup, courtroom reactions, and the legal stakes surrounding one of hip-hop’s most closely watched true crime cases.

--------
Vlad sits down with former Navy SEAL Robert O’Neill and Army Ranger sniper Nicholas “The Reaper” Irving for a candid conversation about sniper training, modern warfare, and fatherhood. O’Neill reflects on graduating sniper school in 1998, the legacy of Marine legend Carlos Hathcock, and why spotting, camouflage, ballistics, wind, and range cards shaped pre-9/11 special warfare. Irving discusses his respect for Hathcock and the impact his own book has had on people wanting to become snipers.

The discussion turns to AI and drones, with both veterans saying today’s technology has changed the battlefield dramatically. When asked whether they’d want their children to follow their path as military snipers, Irving says no, while O’Neill says he’d strongly steer his kids toward military academies, aviation, or competitive shooting instead. The conversation also touches on SEAL Team Six, F-18 pilots, Virginia Beach, Top Gun, Tom Cruise, Denzel Washington, and Man on Fire.
